## TL;DR

Task branches were repeatedly failing landing with "the diff changes another task's bookkeeping": the engineer's self-check WIP checkpoint staged everything dirty in the worktree, and a sibling `work/<other-id>-*.md` (or a report) left dirty by a concurrent board write rode into the branch on every check, re-committing it round after round. This round closed the remaining review findings. The main fix this pass was scoping the handoff's engineering-report commit to its own path so it can never sweep a sibling staged after the restore point; I also deleted a dead `branch.<name>.merge-base` config read in the restore helper, fixed the stale `repoos landable` remediation text that still told engineers to restore files by hand, and reworded the restore docs/messages so "the branch point's copy" matches what the code actually checks out. Enforcement now lives at the commit boundary: every commit in a task worktree is either path-scoped or preceded by an explicit foreign unstage, and handoff heals drift that already landed.

## Work and rationale

The review's first finding was the sharpest: `src/server/handoff.ts` staged the finalized engineering report with `git add -- <reportPath>` and then ran a **bare** `git commit`. That commit runs *after* the check gate — minutes long — while the foreign-bookkeeping restore runs only once, earlier, before the gate. A sibling staged in that window (any `git add -A` in the worktree, a concurrent board write) would ride the report commit onto the branch, and nothing re-ran the restore. I made it `git commit -m <message> -- <reportPath>`. That is valid because the path is already in the index, and `git commit -- <path>` commits only the index entry for that path: I verified in a scratch repo that with `a.txt` and `b.txt` staged, `git commit -- a.txt` commits only `a.txt` and leaves `b.txt` staged. This is the same scoping rule the rest of the branch already follows (the WIP checkpoint commits intended paths; `guardReviewTransition` clears the index then selectively unstages; merge-time commits unstage first because git refuses a partial commit during a merge).

The second finding was a **dead fallback**: `restoreForeignTaskBookkeepingFromMain` read `branch.<name>.merge-base`, but a repo-wide grep found no writer, and the comment claiming "written when RepoOS cut the worktree" was false. The `merge-base <baseBranch> HEAD` fallback was what always ran. I deleted the dead branch and the now-unused `branch --show-current` call, and rewrote the comment to explain why the merge-base (and not the main checkout's current branch tip) is the correct anchor: if main is checked out on another branch, the merge-base from the wrong tip could miss a foreign file present in both trees.

The third finding was **stale remediation text** (criterion 4). `src/core/landable.ts` told the engineer to run `git checkout main -- <path>` by hand — the manual fix the spec and `AGENTS.md` say is never needed now that handoff heals drift. I changed the `nextStep` to say handoff restores the file automatically and to re-request review, and added a table-driven assertion in `landable.test.ts` that locks the new wording in.

I also handled the review's edge case: the restore checks out the copy at the **branch point** (the merge-base with main), not main's tip, because the branch's own diff is graded `merge-base..HEAD`; that is correct and safe, but the commit message and several docs said "main's copy". Rather than leave a false description, I reworded the commit message, the error strings, the helper's doc comment, and the `docs/close-out-pipeline.md` / `docs/agent-workflow-rules.md` / `AGENTS.md` entries to "the branch point's copy", and spelled out why. I also tightened the two docs that said landable "names the fix" to say handoff restores automatically.

## Approaches tried

For the review's suggestion — a `finalizeReviewHandoff` test with a sibling staged before the report commit — I first staged a sibling through the public entry point and found it was cleaned by `guardReviewTransition`'s blanket `reset HEAD -- .`, so it never reached the report commit; the test passed even with the bare commit restored. That was a false pass. I then used the test-only `onProgress` sink: `onProgress("check")` fires after the commit gate's unstage and before the report commit, which is exactly the live window. Staging a *new*, never-committed sibling there reproduced the bug precisely — the test failed on the bare commit (the sibling appeared in the report commit) and passed with the pathspec. I also had to correct the commit lookup (`git show --grep` is a no-op; `git log --grep -1` then `git show <sha>` is the right shape).

The earlier rounds had already landed the broader machinery this pass builds on: the scoped WIP checkpoint (`commitWipCheckpointForRemoteGate` commits `-- <paths>` after resetting foreign bookkeeping), the `guardReviewTransition` foreign unstage, the `restoreForeignTaskBookkeepingFromMain` handoff heal, the lockfile-conflict unstage, and `dropDistBeforeMerge`.

## Challenges and blockers

The hardest part was proving the fix rather than assuming it. My first integration test passed with the fix reverted, which would have shipped a test that guards nothing. Finding the true window required reading the handoff ordering closely (guard → check gate → report commit) and noticing that the guard already clears the index, so the only way to stage a sibling in the window is *after* the guard — which the `onProgress` sink exposes. I deliberately verified the test fails without the fix before keeping it.

A secondary challenge was scope discipline in the docs. "main's copy" appeared in several places with slightly different meanings (the close-out reset really does use main's tip; the handoff restore uses the branch point). I reworded only the handoff-restore mentions and left the close-out ones, so the two mechanisms still read as distinct.

## Key learnings

- A commit made late in a long pipeline needs its own pathspec; "the index was clean earlier" is not a guarantee. Defense in depth at every commit boundary is what the accepted scope requires.
- A config read with no writer is worse than no read: it is a comment that lies. Grepping for the writer before trusting a fallback saved a wrong assumption.
- A regression test must be shown to fail without the fix. An integration test that passes in both states is documentation, not a guard.
